classroom.page.srSummary: An animated figure. A red dot stands for {a_person} with an example task: using a library new to them, fetch three records at the same time. Six cards stand for sections of the library's docs: retry on error, task groups, timeouts, error handling, fetching records and channels. {The_person} reads each section closely, then has an AI write the code, which joins the sections with five grey connections at once. {The_person} takes the code as written, without asking how it works, and hands it in, titled "Fetch all three records in one task group", whose main link is between sections 2 and 5, with a note that AI helped with the code. {A_second}, with the same docs and the same time limit, asks the AI only how cancellation works. The AI explains that in a task group one error cancels all the other tasks, and writes no code. {The_person} writes three connections of their own, then a fourth, between sections 1 and 2, that breaks, with the note "Bug: when one fetch failed, the group canceled the rest." {The_person} fixes it alone: each fetch catches its own error (1 to 4), and a timeout counts as an error (3 to 4). Both hand in the same code within the time limit. In class, with the code closed, both sketch the same connections: the first redrawn from the AI's code, the second built, broken once and fixed. {reviewer_points} to the connection between sections 2 and 5, the task group and the fetches: what would make that fail? {The_first} says, "It fetches all three in one group. If the group fails, they all fail." The second, remembering the bug, says, "A missing record. Its fetch fails, so the group cancels the other two." The figure ends on the {check_l}, with the source under the picture. Each beat is listed below with what is on screen.

classroom.page.setup: Two {people} in a programming course get the same docs and the same time limit to build a feature with a library new to them. The course allows AI, and both say they used it. One takes an AI's code as written, without asking how it works. The other asks the AI only how things work, then writes the code, breaks it once and fixes it. The first route is premature synthesis: the model connects the material before anyone has built the map. What separates them is engaging with how the code works: asking, trying, breaking it and seeing why. Writing it yourself is one way to do that. In the study, the top group had the AI write the code, then asked it follow-up questions to understand it. Illustration based on Shen & Tamkin (2026), a study of developers learning a new library; the {people}, the course and the task are constructed.
classroom.page.editionNote: Classroom edition. PME is the example from the original essay, linked below.
classroom.page.evidence.0: Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin at Anthropic ran a randomized experiment with 52 developers recruited online, most of them professional or freelance programmers: 29 had seven or more years of coding experience, 19 had four to six, and 4 had one to three. They were learning "a new asynchronous programming library", Trio. Each had up to 35 minutes for two short tasks, one of them a function that handles missing-record errors, then took a quiz on the library. Most of the study's participants were working developers; the {people} in the figure are constructed.
classroom.page.evidence.1: Developers given an AI assistant scored lower. The paper puts it this way: "For a 27-point quiz, this translates into a 17% score difference or 2 grade points" (Cohen's d = 0.738, p = 0.01). Anthropic's summary gives the averages as 50% with AI and about 67% by hand. The AI did not make them significantly faster. The average hides a split by how people used the AI: the top-scoring group also had the AI write code, then asked how it worked (below). The authors also note a limit: "there was not the same incentive to learn the library as if it were required for their actual job."
classroom.page.evidence.5: Limits: one session of two short tasks, about an hour, with the quiz straight after; 52 people, and groups of two to seven; and the incentive gap the authors note (above). The figure's question in class is constructed; the study measured a quiz. Other evidence points the other way: a field study of 5,172 customer support agents found "evidence that AI assistance facilitates worker learning" (Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, "Generative AI at Work").

evidence: Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin at Anthropic ran a randomized experiment with 52 developers recruited online, most of them professional or freelance programmers: 29 had seven or more years of coding experience, 19 had four to six, and 4 had one to three. They were learning "a new asynchronous programming library", Trio. Each had up to 35 minutes for two short tasks, one of them a function that handles missing-record errors, then took a quiz on the library.

Developers given an AI assistant scored lower. The paper puts it this way: "For a 27-point quiz, this translates into a 17% score difference or 2 grade points" (Cohen's d = 0.738, p = 0.01). Anthropic's summary gives the averages as 50% with AI and about 67% by hand. The AI did not make them significantly faster.

In an exploratory breakdown ("exploratory data analysis (not pre-registered)"), the largest score gap was on debugging questions. The authors' explanation is that the group without AI "encountered more errors during the task and became more capable at debugging."

How people used the AI mattered, in small groups the authors identified from screen recordings. Conceptual Inquiry, seven people: they "only asked conceptual questions and relied on their improved understanding to complete the task. Although this group encountered many errors, they also independently resolved these errors." They averaged 65%. AI Delegation, four people, "wholly relied on AI to write code and complete the task" and averaged 39%; they were the fastest, at 19.5 minutes on average to Conceptual Inquiry's 22. Iterative AI Debugging, four people, "relied on AI to debug or verify their code" and averaged 24%.

Who wrote the code wasn't the dividing line. The top group, Generation-Then-Comprehension, two people, "first generated code and then manually copied or pasted the code into their work. After their code was generated, they then asked the AI assistant follow-up questions to improve understanding." They averaged 86%. The authors note that this approach "looks nearly the same as the AI delegation group, but additionally uses AI to check their own understanding." In the figure, {the_first} follows AI Delegation, taking the code as written, and the second follows Conceptual Inquiry.

Limits: one session of two short tasks, about an hour, with the quiz straight after; 52 people, and groups of two to seven; and, as the authors note, "there was not the same incentive to learn the library as if it were required for their actual job." The figure's review question is constructed; the study measured a quiz. Other evidence points the other way: a field study of 5,172 customer support agents found "evidence that AI assistance facilitates worker learning" (Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, "Generative AI at Work").
